units.text: In this video, you'll decide when to use Step Functions and how it calls other services. Follow the example: a Lambda task runs first, then a Choice routes to a Dynamo D B task or a wait. The state machine owns the flow; the tasks do the work.

A caught failure can route to the modeled failure path. Standard records execution state and history, while an execution role grants only the downstream calls required. Choose Standard or Express by duration, execution semantics and available patterns.

A state machine turns service calls and decisions into an explicit workflow. The input reaches a Task and a Choice; one branch waits before continuing, while the other fails. Follow the history of a Standard execution to see which branch actually ran.

Amazon States Language defines states and transitions. Passed state data and execution history aid coordination and diagnosis, but the application still stores durable business records in its data services. A single Lambda invocation can execute code; it is not the orchestration shown here.

Pick a service integration by what must happen before the next state. Request-response waits for the service A P I response, not necessarily for the submitted job to finish. A supported optimized job-run integration can instead wait for job completion and requires Standard.

A Standard callback task pauses until an authorized worker returns the task token with success or failure. A W S S D K integrations support request-response and, when the A P I can carry the token, callback; they do not support the job-run pattern.

An approved caller needs permission to start the state machine. For the Standard example, Start Execution returns the execution A R N before the workflow finishes. Synchronous Express uses a separate A P I when the caller needs to wait for the result.

The workflow then uses its own execution role, not the caller's role, to invoke Lambda, send an S Q S message or write Dynamo D B. Scope each downstream action and resource to the tasks defined by the workflow.

In this video, you'll choose workflow states and match the execution type to a real requirement. A Task does work, Wait delays the flow, and Choice branches on input. In the order example, the chosen branch determines how fulfillment proceeds.

Use Parallel for known branches such as updating inventory and sending a notification. Use Map for the same work over a list, such as processing each order item. Choose concurrency and failure behavior to match the downstream capacity.

Standard supports durable execution for up to one year, with a default exactly-once workflow model. Configured retries can repeat a task, so protect business side effects. Long waits or a supported job-run or callback pattern are reasons to choose Standard.

Express supports short, high-volume workflows up to five minutes. Asynchronous Express uses at-least-once execution; synchronous Express uses at-most-once. Neither supports the job-run or callback pattern. Use idempotent work where repeated delivery is possible.

In this video, you'll decide which failures to retry and how to pause for a human decision. Start with Retry: the configured interval, backoff and maximum retry attempts apply to matching errors. A successful attempt continues the workflow; make the underlying operation safe to repeat.

After an eligible retry is exhausted, a matching Catch can route to recovery or compensation. An uncaught error can fail the workflow. The Succeed and Fail states shown are terminal, and an external rollback is work you model, not an automatic undo.

Use a Standard callback task when an external approval must determine the next step. The workflow passes a task token through S Q S to an authorized application, which presents the decision. The application returns the result using Send Task Success or Send Task Failure.

Keep task tokens out of logs and return them only from an authorized principal in the same A W S account. Set an appropriate timeout and heartbeat where needed. A failure callback fails the task, which a matching Catch can still handle if the workflow defines one.

In this video, you'll use S Q S to absorb bursts, then choose between Standard and first in, first out delivery. The producer sends at its own rate, and the consumer processes at its own rate. Acknowledging a queue write means the message was accepted, not that processing finished.

Standard offers at-least-once delivery with best-effort ordering; first in, first out orders within a message group and deduplicates eligible sends. After receiving a message, a worker deletes it only after success. Visibility and a dead-letter queue handle different points in the failure path.

A burst of requests doesn't need to become a burst of database writes. The A P I enqueues work quickly; as the backlog grows, workers drain it at a rate that respects downstream capacity. The producer's acknowledgment is not the Dynamo D B write result.

Make the consumer safe to retry, for example by recording a stable request I D with a conditional write. Watch the visible backlog and oldest-message age on CloudWatch. Investigate repeated failures in the dead-letter queue rather than increasing workers blindly.

Standard S Q S can deliver a message more than once and can deliver messages out of order. The business effect must not depend on a single delivery. In this Dynamo D B example, make the conditional write itself the durable business change. If the work crosses systems, use a durable handoff or an independently idempotent downstream call, not just a processed marker.

Design for a crash after the durable write but before message deletion. On redelivery, the same operation I D can show the write already happened. Acknowledge or delete the message after verifying the durable result, without applying the change a second time.

first in, first out ordering applies within one message group. Give operations that must be ordered for the same order or customer the same group I D. Independent groups can progress concurrently; first in, first out does not give a global order across groups.

A stable deduplication I D suppresses duplicate sends within the five-minute deduplication window. This is separate from what happens if a consumer crashes after a write. Keep consumer-side idempotency even with first in, first out.

In this video, you'll handle message visibility, retention and failures without repeating successful work. Receive makes a message temporarily invisible; successful processing is followed by Delete Message. If it isn't deleted before visibility expires, another worker can receive it.

Long polling waits up to twenty seconds for available messages and reduces empty receives. It is not extra time to process a message after receiving it. Choose visibility to fit the work, and extend it for longer jobs when appropriate.

Separate the queue clocks: a delay postpones initial eligibility, visibility protects an in-flight receive, and retention determines how long S Q S keeps the message. Retention is four days by default and configurable from one minute to fourteen days; delivery delay is up to fifteen minutes.

A native S Q S message can carry up to one mebibyte. For larger data, store it in S three and send a scoped reference instead. The consumer needs permission and a lifecycle plan for the object; deleting the queue message does not automatically delete the object.

A redrive policy sends repeatedly received messages to an eligible dead-letter queue after the configured receive threshold. Inspect the failed message and fix the cause before redriving it. Set compatible queue types and enough retention to support investigation.

Redrive a controlled set and monitor age, backlog and the resulting writes. A redrive is new processing, not an automatic rollback, and it must not duplicate side effects from attempts that already committed.

With Lambda, the event source mapping polls S Q S and delivers a batch to the function. Without partial batch response, a failed batch can become visible again after visibility expires. With Report Batch Item Failures, return the failed IDs and let the successful messages be removed.

For first in, first out, stop processing after the first failure and return both the failed message and unprocessed messages to preserve order. The function and queue must be in the same A W S Region, and an idempotent consumer is still needed.
